items.stem: Which of the following statements regarding social issues in the post-Civil War 19th century is true?
options: African Americans struggled against discriminatory practices even though the case of Plessy v. Ferguson technically outlawed legal segregation.
While African Americans and women achieved suffrage during this period, both groups were often kept from voting through various illegal means.
Impoverished southerners, both Black and white, had greater opportunities for upward mobility than did their northern counterparts due to sharecropping and the crop lien system.
The influx of immigrant factory workers and the development of mass transportation caused the middle class to largely flee the major cities.
items.explanation: In the post-war 19th century the Industrial Revolution caused an influx in many major cities of poor immigrants seeking low-paying factory jobs. Parts of these cities became overcrowded, economically depressed, and crime-ridden, and many middle-class Americans, aided by modern transportation systems, consequently fled the areas—keep (D). African Americans struggled against discrimination and segregation, and the case of Plessy v. Ferguson facilitated such unfair treatment, holding that “separate but equal” accommodations were constitutional, so (A) is incorrect. While Black men were granted the right to vote in 1870, no woman of any race could vote until the Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920, granting suffrage to all women. Choice (B) is incorrect. Sharecropping, based on the crop lien system, served to keep poor farmers, both Black and white, in constant debt and offered little opportunity to improve one’s lot, so (C) is incorrect.

option_explanations.A: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) did not outlaw segregation — it upheld it. The 'separate but equal' ruling gave constitutional cover to Jim Crow laws, making legal segregation worse, not better.
option_explanations.B: Black men gained suffrage with the 15th Amendment (1870), but women did not achieve suffrage in this period — the 19th Amendment came in 1920. The claim that both groups 'achieved suffrage' is false for women.
option_explanations.C: Sharecropping and the crop-lien system trapped poor Southerners in cycles of debt; they did not create greater upward mobility than the North offered. If anything, they locked Black and white tenants in poverty.
option_explanations.D: Industrial cities filled with poor immigrant factory workers became overcrowded and crime-ridden, while new mass transit (streetcars, subways) let the middle class move out — the flight to the suburbs.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about Supreme Court decisions during the latter part of the 19th century is most accurate?
options: They reduced federal power over the states by narrowly defining the applicability of the Constitution to state law.
They cleared the way for the liberal reforms of the 20th century by broadly interpreting constitutional guarantees of individual rights.
They had little practical effect because the executive branch consistently refused to enforce the Court’s rulings.
They used the Fourteenth Amendment to create numerous environmental regulations and human rights, stifling American business growth.
items.explanation: If you remember that the Supreme Court of the late 19th century was extremely conservative and extremely pro-business—and you should remember that, because it’s important—you should have been able to eliminate (B) and (D) immediately. If you remember the profound impact of such decisions as Plessy v. Ferguson —and you should also remember that—you could have eliminated (C).

option_explanations.A: The late-19th-century Court was conservative and pro-business. Decisions like the Civil Rights Cases (1883) and Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) read the 14th Amendment narrowly, shrinking federal power over the states and leaving civil-rights enforcement to them.
option_explanations.B: The Court did not pave the way for liberal reform. It struck down civil-rights protections and sided with business, delaying reform rather than enabling it.
option_explanations.C: These decisions had enormous practical effect — Plessy legitimized Jim Crow for nearly 60 years. They were enforced and obeyed, not ignored by the executive.
option_explanations.D: The Court did not create environmental regulations; that concept barely existed. It used the 14th Amendment mainly to shield businesses from regulation (the coming Lochner era), not to regulate them on environmental or human-rights grounds.

items.stem: The term vertical integration refers to
options: Reconstruction-Era efforts to assimilate newly freed enslaved people into all social strata of American society
an architectural movement that sought to blend urban skyscrapers with the natural landscape surrounding them
the industrial practice of assigning workers a single, repetitive task in order to maximize productivity
control of all aspects of an industry, from production of raw materials to delivery of finished goods
items.explanation: “Vertical integration” is another name for monopoly. Monopolies ran rampant in the late 1800s; the government did little to prevent them, and the courts actively encouraged them. Of the incorrect answers, (C) refers to assembly line production, and (A) and (B) are just made up.

option_explanations.A: This is invented. Reconstruction-era assimilation of freed people has nothing to do with the term 'vertical integration.'
option_explanations.B: This is invented. There was no architectural movement by that name blending skyscrapers with nature.
option_explanations.C: Assigning workers a single repetitive task is assembly-line production (division of labor), not vertical integration. Vertical integration is about owning stages of an industry, not organizing workers' tasks.
option_explanations.D: Vertical integration means one company controls every stage of its industry — for example, Carnegie's steel empire owning the iron mines, railroads, and mills that fed its furnaces, from raw material to finished goods.

items.stem: The passage of the Pendleton Act was a direct result of the
options: assassination of Abraham Lincoln
failure of Reconstruction
assassination of James A. Garfield
Supreme Court decision in Plessy v. Ferguson
items.explanation: James A. Garfield’s presidency is remembered for one thing: Garfield’s assassination at the hands of a disgruntled office seeker. His assassin, Charles Guiteau, was actually a mentally disturbed individual who imagined himself an important player in Garfield’s electoral success. Guiteau convinced himself that he deserved a big fat government job as a reward for his efforts, and when he received none he retaliated by shooting Garfield. Garfield’s successor, Chester Arthur, signed the Pendleton Act, which replaced the spoils system Guiteau had hoped to exploit with a merit-based system for selecting civil servants.

option_explanations.A: Lincoln's assassination (1865) brought Andrew Johnson to the presidency, but it did not produce civil-service reform. The Pendleton Act came 18 years later, from a different assassination.
option_explanations.B: The end of Reconstruction (1877) was a political turning point, but the direct trigger of the Pendleton Act was the spoils-system scandal exposed by Garfield's murder, not Reconstruction's failure.
option_explanations.C: Garfield was shot in 1881 by Charles Guiteau, a mentally disturbed office-seeker furious at being denied a patronage job. The scandal discredited the spoils system, and Garfield's successor Chester Arthur signed the Pendleton Act (1883), creating merit-based federal hiring.
option_explanations.D: Plessy v. Ferguson was decided in 1896, thirteen years after the Pendleton Act — the wrong era and an unrelated subject.

items.stem: The Haymarket Riot represented a major setback for the
options: women’s suffrage movement
civil rights movement for African Americans
Knights of Labor
temperance movement
items.explanation: Although one might certainly make a valid claim that labor unions were necessary during the late 19th century when working conditions were dangerous, unsanitary, and exploitative, unions were very unpopular because they were associated with political radicalism and violence. The 1886 Haymarket Riot began at a mass meeting organized by anarchists in Haymarket Square, Chicago, to protest events related to a strike at the nearby McCormick Harvester Company plant. When police tried to break up the meeting, someone threw a bomb into the crowd, leaving seven police officers dead and several wounded. This incident convinced the American public that unions were dangerous and ultimately led to the decline of the Knights of Labor.

option_explanations.A: The Haymarket affair was a labor rally in Chicago, not a women's-suffrage event. The suffrage movement was not the casualty here.
option_explanations.B: The rally concerned labor issues — the eight-hour day and the McCormick Harvester strike — not African American civil rights.
option_explanations.C: The 1886 Haymarket bombing, at a rally called by anarchists, fused labor unions with radicalism and violence in the public mind. The Knights of Labor, then America's largest union, lost most of its membership in the backlash.
option_explanations.D: The temperance movement had nothing to do with Haymarket Square. Prohibitionists were not involved in the labor rally or the bombing.

items.stem: Japan was outraged by the American annexation of Hawaii in 1898 primarily because
options: Japan depended heavily on trade with Hawaii to support its economy
the United States had signed a treaty with Japan granting Japan rights to Hawaii
the Japanese were committed to the principle of self-rule throughout the Pacific
nearly half of Hawaii’s residents were of Japanese descent
items.explanation: If you can’t immediately identify the correct answer to this one, use common sense to eliminate incorrect answers. Japan is a huge nation relative to Hawaii; its economy couldn’t realistically depend on trade with the island, so eliminate (A). Choice (B) contradicts one of the main themes of the period—the Age of Imperialism, when every Western power, including the United States, was gathering colonies in the East. Would the United States have ceded Hawaii to Japan during that period? Unlikely, and much less likely still that the AP Exam would ask about an anomalous agreement. Choice (C) suggests Japan was a bastion of democracy in the late 19th century; in fact, it was ruled by an emperor.

option_explanations.A: Japan's large industrializing economy did not depend on trade with tiny Hawaii. The economic-dependence story does not fit the relative sizes.
option_explanations.B: No such treaty existed. In the Age of Imperialism the United States was collecting Pacific possessions, not signing them away to Japan.
option_explanations.C: Japan was not a champion of Pacific self-rule — it was building its own empire and would soon take Korea and expand into China. Anti-imperialist principle does not explain its anger.
option_explanations.D: Japanese plantation laborers made up a huge share of Hawaii's population — roughly two-fifths by the 1890s — so Tokyo saw annexation as a direct blow to the rights and interests of its nationals.

items.stem: The “new immigrants” who arrived in the United States after the Civil War were different from the “old immigrants” in that they
options: came mostly from Latin American countries
settled in rural areas in the Midwest where land was plentiful
were better prepared than previous immigrants had been to face the challenges of urban life
came from southern and eastern Europe, speaking unfamiliar languages
items.explanation: Historians describe the immigrants who came to the United States before the Civil War as “old immigrants.” These groups came predominantly from countries in northwestern Europe. For the most part, they were Protestants and spoke English and easily became part of the melting pot we call America. Following the Civil War, however, the “new immigrants” came predominantly from nations in South and Eastern Europe, including Russians, Italians, and Poles. Many of these people were Catholics and Jews and were culturally very different from most Americans by that point. These new immigrants were not easily assimilated. They tended to settle among themselves in ethnic neighborhoods in major cities like New York and Chicago where there was a demand for unskilled labor in the numerous factories of these big cities.

option_explanations.A: Large-scale Latin American immigration came later, in the 20th century. The post-Civil War 'new immigrants' were Europeans.
option_explanations.B: The new immigrants settled overwhelmingly in industrial cities, not on Midwestern farms. Rural Midwestern settlement was characteristic of the earlier 'old' immigrants (Germans, Scandinavians).
option_explanations.C: The new immigrants were less prepared, not more: many were poor, spoke no English, and were Catholic or Jewish in a largely Protestant country — which is exactly why they faced a nativist backlash.
option_explanations.D: After the Civil War the immigrant stream shifted to southern and eastern Europe — Italians, Poles, Russians, and eastern-European Jews — speaking unfamiliar languages and culturally distinct from earlier arrivals.

items.stem: The “Ghost Dance” movement among Western Native Americans stressed all of the following EXCEPT
options: the belief that the world would soon come to an end
the rejection of alcohol and other trappings of white society
unity among Native Americans of different tribes
nonviolence
items.explanation: The Ghost Dancers arose in the late 1800s when the sad fate awaiting the great Native American tribes of the era was becoming all too apparent. Wovoka, of the Paiute people, started the Ghost Dance movement, which resembled a religious revival. It centered on a dance ritual that enabled participants to envision a brighter future, one in which white people no longer dominated North America. Wovoka preached unity among Native Americans and the rejection of white culture and its trappings, especially alcohol. He also preached the imminent end of the world, at which point the Native American dead would rise to reclaim the land that was rightfully theirs. Sioux Ghost Dancers believed in the power of “ghost shirts,” garments blessed by spiritual leaders that were capable of stopping bullets. This belief led to a rise in Sioux militancy and ultimately contributed to their massacre at Wounded Knee in 1890.

option_explanations.A: Wovoka, the Paiute prophet who began the movement, preached that the world would soon end and be renewed, with the Native dead returning and white dominance erased — so this was a stressed tenet, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: The movement explicitly called for rejecting white culture and its trappings, especially alcohol — so this was a stressed tenet, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Wovoka preached unity across tribal lines, and the dance spread from tribe to tribe — so intertribal unity was a stressed tenet, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Nonviolence was not one of the movement's defining tenets. The Ghost Dance centered on the coming renewal, the rejection of white ways, and Native unity — and as it spread, especially among the Lakota, it took on a militant cast that alarmed the U.S. Army, ending in the Wounded Knee massacre of 1890.

items.stem: In the late 19th century, political machines such as Tammany Hall were successful primarily because
options: they operated primarily in rural areas, where the government could not monitor their activities
they focused on accomplishing only a narrow set of human rights objectives
they championed the suffragettes and received their support in return
machine politicians provided needed jobs and services to naturalized citizens in return for their votes
items.explanation: Waves of European immigration throughout the 19th century swelled cities’ populations. Governments of the time were nowhere near as activist as they are today, and only a very few provided even minimal services to immigrants as they accommodated themselves to their new homeland; ethnic communities and churches were expected to provide such services. A number of enterprising, unscrupulous men recognized the opportunity to develop great political power with these immigrants. Such men, known as political bosses, helped immigrants find homes and jobs and acquire citizenship and voting rights. In essence, these bosses created entire communities and then provided them with all sorts of services: food and loans for the poor, parks and protection for the community. In return, the communities were expected to provide loyal political support, which they did, originally out of loyalty, and later, as the machines became extremely powerful, out of both loyalty and fear. The bosses could then hand an election to a politician of their choice, in return for favors. Political machines filled a need, albeit in an expensive and unethical way. They fell from power when governments started to provide many of the services machines had provided.

option_explanations.A: Political machines were urban, not rural. Bosses like Tweed operated in big cities where immigrants concentrated — Tammany Hall was New York City's Democratic machine.
option_explanations.B: Machines were not human-rights organizations. They traded patronage for power; their 'objectives' were votes and control, not rights campaigns.
option_explanations.C: Machines did not champion suffragettes. Their base was immigrant men who could vote; women could not yet vote in most states, so machines had no reason to back their cause.
option_explanations.D: City governments provided almost no services to immigrants, so bosses filled the gap: jobs, housing help, and assistance with citizenship and voting — in exchange for votes on Election Day.

items.stem: All of the following states were admitted to the union in the post-war 19th century EXCEPT
options: North Dakota
Wyoming
Arizona
Washington
items.explanation: Arizona was not admitted to the union until 1912.

option_explanations.A: North Dakota was admitted in 1889 — in the post-war 19th century, so it is not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Wyoming was admitted in 1890 — in the post-war 19th century, so it is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Arizona was not admitted until 1912, in the 20th century — making it the exception.
option_explanations.D: Washington was admitted in 1889 — in the post-war 19th century, so it is not the exception.

items.stem: Which of the following was NOT associated with the westward expansion of railroads during the mid- to late 19th century?
options: The social doctrine of Manifest Destiny
Increased confrontation between settlers and Western Native American tribes
The economic decline and loss of political influence of Tammany Hall
The emergence of the Populist movement
items.explanation: The westward expansion of the United States (driven by newly acquired lands from the Mexican Cession and the Gadsden Purchase) during the mid- to late 19th century was quickly aided by the expansion of railroads and the desire and perceived right of Americans to explore and settle the West consistent with the doctrine of Manifest Destiny. One result of this expansion was increased confrontation between settlers and tribes. Ultimately, the power and influence of railroad magnates such as Vanderbilt led to the emergence of political movements to regulate the railroads, such as the Grange movement and the later Populist movement. Tammany Hall was based in New York and had little to do with westward expansion.

option_explanations.A: Manifest Destiny — the belief that Americans were destined to settle the continent — was the ideological engine of railroad expansion westward. It is directly associated.
option_explanations.B: Railroads carried settlers west in huge numbers, intensifying competition for land and conflict with Western tribes. It is directly associated.
option_explanations.C: Tammany Hall was a New York City political machine. Its fortunes had nothing to do with western railroads — this is the one item not associated with railroad expansion.
option_explanations.D: Railroad abuses, especially discriminatory freight rates, helped spark the Grange and then the Populist movement, which demanded railroad regulation. It is directly associated.
